examples.title: 25 practical minutes do not contain the wait
examples.situation: A student collects Plot C soil at 10:00, starts air drying, and later begins the example’s 30–60-minute pH equilibration.
reasoning: The planned 25-minute practical block is an active-work planning figure; it cannot include every necessary dry/equilibrate interval.
Record one sample ID across collection, drying, pH, feel and later reporting, with actual date/time for each action.
The student carries out each task; a trainer's earlier example tube is demonstration only.
examples.takeaway: Staged observed work with active and waiting times logged separately; no shortcut pass.

examples.title: Two cups are not a mass reading
examples.situation: The example says submit 'about 2 cups or 500 grams' of the composite.
reasoning: Ask what amount and unit the receiving lab actually requests.
If it requires 500 g, weigh that amount; if it requests two cups, measure volume and label it as such.
Record the sample ID and required sampling depth/count rather than equating volume with mass.
examples.takeaway: One unambiguous measured submission amount and an intact identity chain.

examples.title: A ratio must name its basis
examples.situation: The teaching example uses 20 g dry soil plus 20 mL distilled water: mass:volume. A separate laboratory method uses 1:1 volume:volume, taking soil with the scoop named ‘10 gram NCR-13 volumetric scoop’ and adding 10 mL deionized water. That is a volumetric scoop's name, not an instruction to weigh exactly 10 g of this soil.
reasoning: The worked example is mass:volume; the lab example is volume:volume.
Choose the actual training SOP and meter, then log its aliquot, wait and calibration; do not borrow an attractive number from the other procedure.
A digital-electrode measurement and a colour-reagent comparison use different equipment and procedures; one does not demonstrate the other.
examples.takeaway: A reproducible, device-matched measurement rather than a mixed-method number.

examples.title: The same short ribbon may mean different classes
examples.situation: Two samples both produce a 2 cm ribbon, but one feels gritty and the other feels very smooth when wet rubbed.
reasoning: Confirm proper moisture and ball/ribbon conditions first.
Follow the USDA weak-ribbon branch, then distinguish gritty from smooth wet-rub feel.

If the weak-ribbon sample feels very gritty, the guide supports sandy loam; if it feels very smooth, it supports silt loam. If neither feel predominates, use the loam branch. These remain conditional field estimates.
examples.takeaway: Classify with both ribbon length and feel; note field-estimate uncertainty.
